maths.title: Counting & number
maths.subtitle: Names for how many
summary: Numbers describe size, order and position. Different societies built different symbols and counting systems.
details: What counts as known: A definition or theorem is known mathematics only with explicit assumptions and a valid proof. Checking many examples is not a proof for every case.
Where it began: Counting and measurement developed across many cultures; there is no single inventor of "numbers".

maths.title: Place-value notation
maths.subtitle: Position carries value
summary: The value of a digit depends on its position. This makes large numbers and efficient calculation much easier.
details: Examples: Babylonian mathematics used base 60; decimal place value with zero developed in India and travelled through other mathematical traditions.
Careful credit: Place-value systems arose independently in more than one place; the story is not one straight chain of invention.

maths.title: P versus NP
maths.subtitle: Easy to check means easy to solve?
summary: P is efficiently solvable decision problems; NP is decision problems with efficiently verifiable certificates. Does P = NP?
details: Not a speed benchmark: "Efficient" has a precise polynomial-time meaning here. NP does not stand for "not polynomial".
Consequences: If one NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm then all NP problems do. No accepted general resolution is known.

maths.title: Kepler conjecture
maths.subtitle: The densest sphere packing — solved
summary: No packing of equal spheres in ordinary three-dimensional space has greater density than the face-centred cubic arrangement.
details: Density: The maximum density is π/√18, about 74%. The proof combines geometry with extensive computation.
Formal checking: The Flyspeck project later produced a formal proof of the result. Publication and formal proof are related but distinct milestones.
